source.title: Data pruning and neural scaling laws: fundamental limitations of score-based algorithms

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper gives theoretical and empirical results about how data pruning affects performance as the retained sample size changes, including an explicit finding of multi-phase scaling on a synthetic dataset. This refines the scope of scaling-law claims but does not test language-model pretraining laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior scaling-law results, which are not recorded as findings of this study. Rows below cover Figure 10's own synthetic-dataset test-error scaling experiments. Logistic-regression performance-gap plots and image-recognition comparisons concern pruning performance but do not report the scaling-law result represented by these rows.
record.test_reason: The paper studies whether score-based data pruning can beat sample-size power-law scaling. It uses the power law only as a reference curve and reports pruning methods' test error relative to random pruning. Experiments use a 3-layer MLP on synthetic classification data, plus ResNets on CIFAR. No power law is fitted, no exponents are reported, and no language-model loss is measured. The Figure 10 curves are figure-only. The one shape remark, multi-phase curves on the nonlinear datasets, is stated as a visual impression for a non-LM toy system. So no version is tested on its own terms. That remark is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors prove No-Free-Lunch results: score-based pruning algorithms are non-consistent, and label-dependent ones are non-valid at small compression levels. Hence they underperform random pruning there and cannot improve scaling laws without adaptation. Their exact calibration protocol restores validity (the error gap vanishes with enough data). It does not systematically beat random pruning, and whether calibration can beat power-law scaling is left open.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes and empirically evaluates data-pruning procedures and test error versus subset size; it does not reproduce the language-model scaling experiments or fitting procedure of the cited original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling behavior changes with dataset and pruning method; high-compression GraNd performance is especially poor on nonlinear and noisy data. Figure 10 uses r ∈ {0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1}.

fits_no_version.finding: On synthetic Nonlinear datasets with a 3-layer MLP, test error vs subset size shows visually identified multi-phase behaviour (two phases, each a different power law). No fits are reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data-size scaling curves of small networks on synthetic tasks can be piecewise power laws rather than a single power law.

fits_no_version.finding: Score-based pruning (GraNd) degrades data-size scaling at high compression (r ≤ 0.2) on nonlinear and noisy data, and beats random pruning only on the linear dataset.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Score-based data pruning cannot generally improve sample-size power-law scaling in the high-compression regime.

record.code_released: The authors say the reproduction code will be open-sourced soon; no URL for their code is stated. The DeepCore code they acknowledge is at https://github.com/PatrickZH/DeepCore.
record.problems: The scaling evidence is on synthetic classification tasks with a single stated MLP architecture, not language models. Figure 10 provides plotted values without numerical extraction or reported fit parameters. The authors describe the multi-phase pattern as visually identified.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 6 and 7 report logistic-regression performance gaps, not a fitted scaling law. Figures 11 and 12 compare image-classification accuracy across pruning fractions and calibration settings, not performance scaling with subset size. No values from cited prior work are included.

untested.parts: No language-model pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Only figure-only toy MLP data-size curves and CIFAR accuracy vs pruning fraction. There is no fitted power law in any other modality or regime.
No exponents are fitted or compared, and there is no fitting-choice sensitivity analysis. The curve-bending remark is visual and limited to a synthetic MLP.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T5' relation and its V5/V7 labels are not supported. The study is about data-pruning methods. Its scaling evidence is figure-only toy MLP curves without fits, so no verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test held-out language-model pretraining loss against parameter count, training tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits are tested against much larger runs.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is measured.
No comparison of architecture details at a fixed parameter count is reported.

The experiments concern synthetic classification datasets and data pruning, not other modalities such as image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer. They do not establish the form across other training regimes generally.
No downstream-task performance is related to pretraining loss or scale.

The paper does not fit or compare scaling exponents systematically, nor test compute-optimal splits or parameter-counting choices. Its evidence on curve shape is limited to synthetic data-pruning experiments.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Synthetic classification data with data pruning, including the linear, nonlinear, and noisy nonlinear datasets
reader_labels.reason: The observed scaling behavior depends on dataset and pruning method: GraNd can beat power-law scaling on the linear task but performs poorly at high compression on nonlinear tasks; see F10-GRAND-LIN, F10-GRAND-NONLINEAR, and F10-GRAND-NOISY. These experiments do not establish a common power-law form across regimes.
